newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl urges SPD to resume tax reform talks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl urges SPD to resume tax reform talks.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Wednesday urged opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to return to the bargaining table for talks on tax reform.
The SPD boycotted a round of talks slated for last Saturday in protest against the government's plan to slash subsidies to coal miners.

Kohl told a trades' conference, "We have to sit down together." The SPD should resume the tax reform talks without regard for tactical political considerations, and should not link the tax and coal issues, he said.
Both sides agree the comprehensive tax reform planned by Finance Minister Theo Waigel is badly needed to promote investment and boost jobs.
The plan includes a net 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in tax cuts and would greatly simplify the system.
The SPD has urged the government to accelerate the package from its planned 1999 start. But opposition leaders have been busy this week addressing coal miners' rallies that have paralysed Bonn.

SPD party manager Franz Muentefering said on Wednesday the party was willing to resume the tax talks, in the interests of fighting unemployment, even if Kohl's negotiations with coal miners on Thursday produce no agreement.

SPD parliamentary faction leader Rudolf Scharping said the party remained opposed to taxes on night- and holiday shifts. But it was prepared to allow a rise in indirect taxes to finance a cut in non-wage labour costs.
Scharping urged the government to put all subsidies on the bargaining table, not just coal, but agriculture and housing construction as well.
Hans Olaf Henkel, head of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), said a failure to agree on tax reform would have dire consequences for Germany.
But he added in an interview with the Rheinische Merkur he believed the government had already lost too much time to meet its goal of halving unemployment by 2000, even with tax reform.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary faction leader of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), said some transitional arrangement was conceivable on taxes on shift work, but he rejected opposition calls for a government move to stimulate domestic demand.
Kohl said he was open to suggestions on moving up large parts of the package to 1998. But the overall concept should be retained, and the financial basis of the package should be secure.
He added that a failure to talk now would just postpone the issue until autumn, and that Germany could not afford the delay. Germany needed tax reform to remain competitive, he said.
